prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated free of light shifts, bringing optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for the optical lattice clock to Katori and Ye. Round 1 left two options standing, and they do not differ on scientific merit. The Higgs observation is the larger result, and nobody disputes that or its maturity. The difference is whether the prize can credit it defensibly, and there the exchange has made the Higgs case harder, not easier. Seven of eight members ranked B001 at opening and proposed three different trios from the same four names, and the three supporters still disagree with each other in round 1 about the CMS seat. B013 needs no such adjudication, because both the idea and the decisive demonstration have two clear owners. The distinct invention is Katori's magic-wavelength lattice, which lets a large ensemble be held and interrogated at once without Stark shifts, and Ye's group turned that into the 1e-18 systematic uncertainty and the many-body clock physics. Independent confirmation in Sr, Yb and other species across many national laboratories is the maturity evidence I weigh most. The pending redefinition of the second is a supporting consequence and I do not make the case depend on it. I also no longer rest any part of the case on the 2005 and 2012 prizes making this timely: that argument points both ways, and I withdraw it in favour of the argument from distinctness.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes is the real weakness and I do not think it is fully answered. A reader can fairly say that this is the third prize in one metrology tradition, and Wineland's Al+ ion clocks are a parallel route to similar accuracy, so the citation must not imply that lattice clocks alone achieved 1e-18. Attribution for the first demonstrations also includes Takamoto, Lemonde and the Paris group, and the German groups, and a two-name credit is a judgement about the proposal and the record-setting realization. Practical impact is still partly prospective until the second is redefined. Finally, the Higgs discovery remains the larger scientific event, so choosing B013 means placing defensible credit above significance, and I accept that this is a value judgement that members can reasonably make the other way if a Higgs trio can be justified by a stated principle.

responses.point: Eriksson agrees with the scientific case for B013 but says that my appeal to the 2005 prize makes the work timely is also the best argument against its novelty, and that the real argument is that magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms is a new idea absent from the comb and ion-clock work.
responses.response: He is right and I have changed my wording. The comb solved how to count optical cycles and the ion-clock work solved how to control a single trapped ion; neither contained the idea of holding thousands of atoms in a lattice at a wavelength where the clock transition is not shifted. That is what gives lattice clocks their stability advantage, and it is the argument I now put forward. I also accept his view of my disclosure as something to record, and I address it below. Where I would still go beyond him is on the citation: it should describe the magic-wavelength lattice explicitly, so that the prize cannot be read as a general award for precision optical clocks.

responses.point: Danielsson holds that the Higgs discovery has never been experimentally recognised, that B013 continues a metrology line already honoured in 2005 and 2012, and that the four first places for B001 reflect agreement on the discovery but not on the names.
responses.response: I agree with his last point and it supports my position. Four first places for the same discovery with three different trios shows that what the committee has agreed on is the result, not the laureates, and he himself says the choice between Della Negra and Virdee rests on general knowledge that the supplied text does not settle. A discovery where the science is certain but the credit cannot be argued from the record is exactly one where I would rather award the case that can. On the continuation point, I answer that the Academy has recognised the clock tool kit twice because each step solved a different problem, and the lattice clock is a third distinct problem, not a repetition. I do not dismiss his concern, and it is the reason I want the citation worded narrowly.

responses.point: As chair, Pearce moved to a Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee trio, accepts that no three-person choice is uniquely fair, and asks whether the committee prefers founders or announcement-time spokespersons, while rating B013 a refinement of a tradition already honoured, with the redefinition of the second still pending.
responses.response: His founders-versus-spokespersons question is the right one, and my answer to it is that the committee does not have the evidence to answer it. Whichever principle is chosen drops a person who led one of the two experiments, so the outcome is a leadership judgement, which he accepts in his own statement. The comparison with B013 is that its attribution does not depend on choosing a principle at all. I would answer the pending-redefinition point differently from him: the second has not yet been redefined, but optical clocks have already been compared at the 1e-18 level in several laboratories, so the maturity of the science does not wait for the metrological decision. Even if the vote then went to B001, I would not oppose it on merit, only on how defensible the names are.

responses.point: Lindroth agrees on the core case and the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and says the citation should be framed around the neutral-atom lattice and the magic-wavelength idea, not around optical clocks in general.
responses.response: I accept her framing and have moved my citation toward it, naming the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation explicitly. This answers the chair's question on how the citation should separate the work from the comb and the ion clocks: narrow on the lattice and the 1e-18 realization, with no claim about optical clocks in general. It also avoids implying a ranking against the Al+ ion route, which Mehlig rightly says the citation should not claim to have surpassed. Her reservation about wording in my first statement is accepted, because the narrower citation is more accurate and more defensible.

responses.point: Mehlig accepts the physics of B013 but asks that my support be counted with my disclosed link in mind, notes that the case does not rest on my ballot, and rejects timing arguments based on the 2005 prize.
responses.response: I agree with all three points. The case does not depend on my ballot, since five members hold it without me and Mehlig herself ranked it second at opening. I also accept her correction on the 2005 prize, as stated above. Her remark that arbitrary credit is a reason to be cautious rather than a reason to reject the Higgs discovery is the position I now hold: I would support B001 if the committee could state a principle for the three names, and I would then ask whether it is more defensible than B013, but I do not see that principle yet in the record.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B001 with Gianotti, Della Negra and Jenni, keeps Della Negra for the founding conception of CMS, would accept Virdee on a stronger documented case, and says my disclosure does not undermine the clock case, while warning that the 2025 circuit prize is close in time to B054.
responses.response: I appreciate that he treats the choice of Della Negra over Virdee as a judgement, not a fact, and that he lists B013 as his fallback. His warning on proximity matters: together with his own WACQT conflict and my own WACQT ties, it is why I have dropped B054 from my alternatives and replaced it with B046. I do not agree that a Higgs trio can be settled by the founding principle alone, because under it ATLAS gets two seats and CMS one, which Pearce and Danielsson regard as unbalanced, and under announcement-time leadership a different person is omitted. The practical result is that his own fallback is likely to be needed, which I would accept as a good outcome.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that magic-wavelength many-atom trapping is a distinct invention and not a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 lineages; I judge it distinct, but I have no way to prove it from the supplied text.
How the citation can credit Katori's proposal and Ye's realization without suggesting that Takamoto, Lemonde, the Paris group, the German groups or the ion-clock community did not contribute.
Whether the second will have been redefined, or be firmly scheduled, at the time of the decision; I treat this as supporting evidence only.
Whether a principled three-person Higgs configuration exists, since one would change my assessment of the relative defensibility of B001 and B013.
My account of the relative roles of Katori and Ye is recalled from general knowledge and not verified from primary sources.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: this is a possible perceived connection, not a documented conflict. During my doctoral period I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory, and Jun Ye is associated with Hall's group. I have no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye. I also work in atomic physics and quantum optics in the same broad community as the candidates, and I have Lund and WACQT quantum-technology ties, which is why I no longer list B054 as an alternative. The chair asked whether this should be recorded as a recusal question. I would accept that the committee records it and I will follow whatever it decides on recusal for B013. The case for B013 is held by five members independently of my ballot, and my ballot is not needed for it, so a recusal by me would not change the configuration.
